claims.text: Formation and long-term persistence of a protective oxide scale above 900 °C in CrFeCoNiX alloys is governed by preferential oxidation of element X.
Preferential oxidation of X controls diffusion kinetics at the oxide/alloy interface.
Preferential oxidation of X controls lattice coherence at the oxide/alloy interface.
When X is Al, CrFeCoNiAl favors formation of a coherent, low-defect Al2O3 scale.
The Al2O3 scale on the Al-containing alloy grows slowly and adheres strongly to the substrate.
Oxides produced when X is Si or Mn have higher defect densities than the oxide produced when X is Al.
Oxides produced when X is Si or Mn have a larger thermal mismatch with the alloy than the Al-derived oxide.
The higher defect densities and thermal mismatch of Si- or Mn-derived oxides promote cracking and spallation.
Crystallographic match and low thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and alloy mediate oxide-layer coherence.
Oxide/alloy interfacial coherence strongly influences diffusion paths for oxygen and cations.
The thermodynamic stability of Al2O3 contributes to formation of a continuous protective layer.
Low oxygen diffusivity in Al2O3 reduces ionic transport and thereby limits further oxidation.
Si- and Mn-derived oxides are less structurally compatible with the CrFeCoNiX substrate than Al2O3.
Under identical high-temperature exposures, Al-containing alloys will develop thinner, slower-growing oxide scales than Si- or Mn-containing alloys.
Under identical high-temperature exposures, oxide scales on Al-containing alloys will show less cracking and spallation than scales on Si- or Mn-containing alloys.
Si- or Mn-containing alloys may grow oxide scales faster than Al-containing alloys.
A control alloy known to form non-protective oxides will show rapidly growing, non-uniform, and spalled oxide under the same exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to single- or multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions exposed above 900 °C for 100–300 hours in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
